source: Coulthart (2015) dissertation, full abstract via CORE API (Univ. of Pittsburgh)
finding: The full abstract says the systematic review used a random SAMPLE of more than 2,000 studies. It found moderate to strong evidence for three techniques: ACH, brainstorming, devil's advocacy. Three main findings: face-to-face collaboration lowers creativity; evidence weighting seems more important than seeking disconfirming evidence; conflict tends to improve quality. A small experiment (21 graduate intelligence-studies students) confirmed the first two findings.
numbers: Survey of 80 analysts at one agency, 5 expert interviews, 15 follow-up interviews; 1 in 3 analysts never used the techniques. Training predicted use (p=0.001, Cramer's V=0.41); perceived value (p=.049, V=0.23); time pressure did not (p=0.74). Review: more than 2,000 studies sampled; 21 students in the experiment.
quote: evidence weighting appears to be more important than seeking disconfirming evidence
limits: No per-technique effect sizes or study counts appear in the abstract. The 238-page PDF sits behind a Cloudflare bot wall (HTTP 403) and was not read. The 21-student experiment cannot show 'weighing beats seeking' with any power. The headline is a sampled vote count, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: do not cite 'moderate to strong' as an effect size. Treat 'weighing beats seeking' as a weak lead from 21 students plus vote counting.

source: Mandel, Karvetski & Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? (JDM 13(6)) - how it cites Coulthart 2017
finding: The authors quote Coulthart (2017, p. 377), who concluded ACH was 'found to be effective and had a highly credible evidence base', and call that conclusion unwarranted. They say the findings are at best equivocal: Lehner et al. (2008) found ACH cut confirmation bias in non-analysts but not in analysts. One non-peer-reviewed study (Wheaton 2014) found accuracy was best in the no-ACH control group.
numbers: Quote: Coulthart 2017 p.377. Lehner 2008: effect in non-analysts, none in analysts. Wheaton 2014: control best, too little information to interpret.
quote: found to be effective and had a highly credible evidence base
limits: Second-hand view of Coulthart from critics. Wheaton 2014 is unpublished and was not seen.
agent_relevance: The 'ACH has strong support' headline is contested by the analysts' own literature. Do not make ACH a default operator on the strength of Coulthart.

source: Wynn, Satija & Hadfield (2025) Talk isn't always cheap: failure modes in multi-agent debate - Table 1
finding: Debate is compared with the majority vote of the SAME agents' independent first answers (the 'w/o Debate' column). Debate lowered accuracy in most mixed-model groups. On CommonsenseQA debate lowered accuracy in every group tested. Mixing model families did not rescue it.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; 2 debate rounds; 100 random items per task; 5 seeds; mean and SE. Single agents: CSQA 74.8 / 57.0 / 41.6; MMLU 82.6 / 55.6 / 34.0; GSM8K 93.2 / 76.4 / 34.2 (row order GPT, Llama, Mistral inferred). Examples before to after debate, majority vote: one-of-each mixed group CSQA 53.4 to 46.8, MMLU 40.0 to 28.0 (-12.0), GSM8K 61.0 to 64.8 (+3.8); a strong-plus-weak group CSQA 58.2 to 50.2, MMLU 51.8 to 43.6, GSM8K 82.6 to 75.8. Some GSM8K groups gained (+2.8 to +4.4).
limits: Small, cheap models (8B and 7B, plus GPT-4o-mini), 100 items per task. Row labels in the text extract are garbled, so which group each row is was inferred from the order and the caption. Not frontier models. Independent-first is the baseline here, not a treatment.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: the independent-first majority vote is a better default than debate on these tasks, and a mixed-family panel did not fix debate. Keep independent sampling as the baseline and treat any interaction step as something that must beat it.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) Section 6 - flip analysis (social pressure)
finding: Across rounds, correct-to-incorrect answer changes outnumber incorrect-to-correct ones. A correct agent is most likely to flip when it is alone in its answer, and the chance falls as more peers agree. Strong and weak models flip less on GSM8K than the middle model, so the pattern varies by model and task.
numbers: Exact flip rates are shown only in bar figures (Fig 2 to 4), not in a table or text, so no single flip percentage can be quoted. Text: 'most agents with incorrect initial answers do not improve'; correct to incorrect exceeds incorrect to correct in later rounds.
limits: Rates were not recoverable as numbers from the text extract. Only the direction and the isolation effect are firm.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the numeric flip rates stay unrecovered. The isolation effect says a lone correct dissenter is the most likely to be talked out of a right answer. A critic stage should see only the answer, not peer pressure, and the final choice should be made by code from independent samples.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) Section 6.3 - payoff prompt test
finding: Telling the model 'maximize your payoff p = I[X==Y]' (be correct) did not cut correct-to-incorrect flips. In many cases flips increased.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini on CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K; base prompt versus correctness prompt; effect shown in Fig 5 only.
limits: One model and a prompt-level fix only; no figures in numbers.
agent_relevance: An instruction such as 'stay correct' does not stop conformity. A structural fix (blind first answers, code decides) is needed.

source: Lee, Kang & Shin (2026) Make LLMs see like investigators: structured analysis in investigative reasoning (PRISM, ACL 2026)
finding: A four-agent pipeline that filters evidence, builds suspect profiles (motive, means, opportunity, alibi), builds an ACH matrix and then lets an LLM judge decide beat plain prompting on all 10 models. Chain of thought and a detective persona gave nothing. Self-consistency (5 samples) helped some.
numbers: MuSR murder mysteries, 250 items, 2 suspects (chance 50%). Mean accuracy over 10 models: Direct 58.1, CoT 57.2, Persona 58.2, P-CoT 58.0, Self-Consistency 63.2, PRISM 71.3 (+13.2 over Direct; range +6.0 Ministral-8B to +22.0 GPT-5.2). GPT-5.2: 58.0 to 80.0. CoT hurt Llama-3.1-8B and lowered Mixtral-8x7B by 4.8 and Qwen3-14B by 2.0. Temperature 0 except SC at 0.7.
limits: Not equal tokens: PRISM uses four agent calls, SC uses 5 samples, and no token counts are given. The final judge is an LLM, not code-scored. MuSR is synthetic narratives with a single binary answer. Part of the gain is evidence filtering.
agent_relevance: First measured support that a hypothesis-by-evidence structure helps on a culprit task with known answers on current models, but the gain comes mostly from the filtering and profile steps, not the ACH step (see d07).

finding: Removing steps one at a time shows where the gain is. Evidence filtering alone reached 63.8%. Adding the motive-means-opportunity-alibi profiling added +6.7 points. Adding the ACH matrix on top added only +0.8 points (11% of the structure gain).
numbers: Average accuracy over 10 models on MuSR: filter-only 63.8; filter plus profiling +6.7 (89% of the +7.5 structure gain); full PRISM adds ACH +0.8. Filter-only 63.8 is above Self-Consistency 63.2 (5 samples).
limits: The ACH step here is rated by an LLM and judged by an LLM; consistency counting is not weighted by code. +0.8 is an average and no significance test is reported. Only 2 suspects.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partial answer: the ACH matrix step itself added little (+0.8) over structured profiling on a 2-suspect task. A rated matrix may pay off only with more than 2 hypotheses and conflicting items. Test with 4+ hypotheses.

source: Chen et al. (2026) LEAP: Likelihood Elicitation and Aggregation for LLM-based Probabilistic Forecasting
finding: This is the closest test of 'model rates each item, code combines'. The LLM gives a likelihood for each evidence item in isolation. Code applies a prior and a Bayes update. It beat the LLM reading all evidence at once, with the same evidence and a token-matched control.
numbers: Five base models (DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, Claude-Haiku-4.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Grok-4.20-Fast). FutureX score gains 3.6 to 18.1 points; accuracy and Spherical improve on every model; Brier improves on 3 of 5 and is tied on 2. Four external agent CLIs: FutureX +7.0 to +13.8, Brier -12.9 to -23.7 points. Diagnostic subset: Monolithic FX .6512, Brier .2689, ECE .1840; LEAP FX .7284, Brier .2057, ECE .0876. Equal-token control: Monolithic with same prior, two-sample mean (11,753 tokens) FX .6736, Brier .2497, ECE .1471, versus LEAP (11,508 tokens) FX .7284, Brier .2057, ECE .0876.
limits: Task is real-world forecasting and browsing (FutureX, GAIA, BrowseComp), not hypothesis matrices over fixed fact patterns. Authors built the benchmark. Small and mid models, not top frontier. Without the prior, LEAP falls below the plain baseline (.6427 vs .6512), so the prior is essential. Gain grows with horizon (6.8 to 11.9 FX points from 7 to 60 days).
agent_relevance: Gap 1 mostly answered for forecasting: a code-aggregated evidence-rating step beats a plain judge at equal tokens on current models. Not yet shown for a hypothesis matrix on investigation items, and no prompt-only ACH arm was run.

source: Chen et al. (2026) LEAP - dependency clustering ablation and grouping sensitivity
finding: Evidence items from the same source (pages quoting one report) are grouped by a dependency key the model returns, and code keeps one item per group. Turning this off made the posterior too sharp (double counting), hurt accuracy and worsened calibration.
numbers: Diagnostic subset: full LEAP FX .7284, Brier .2057, ECE .0876. Without dependency clustering: FX .7089 (-1.9 points), Brier .2299, ECE .1578. Without reliability sampling: FX .7136, Brier .2215, ECE .1219. Grouping: none 5.12 items kept, FX .7089, Brier .2299, ECE .1578; source-key 4.37 kept (85.3%), FX .7284, Brier .2057, ECE .0876; domain 3.72 kept (72.6%), FX .7192, Brier .2144, ECE .0798.
limits: Dependence is detected by the same LLM (it writes the key), so errors in keys pass through. Only shared-source dependence is handled, not partial or causal overlap. One diagnostic subset.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 answered in part: code-side grouping of correlated evidence helps (about 2 points accuracy, ECE .158 to .088). Copy this: each evidence item carries a source key and code collapses same-source items before scoring.

source: Kawada & Kellis (2026) Evidence integration in large language models (MIT)
finding: Twelve models integrate external answers as a shift of their own answer distribution. Candidates the model already finds likely are more persuasive. Agreement between two distinct messages is sub-additive. An exact repeated message is largely discounted, unlike a distinct second message.
numbers: Over ten million trials, 12 instruction-tuned models from 4 families, 8 domains. Second message's effect is explained by the post-first-message margin with R2 0.39 to 0.74 versus 0.00 to 0.05 for pre-evidence support. Interaction slope -0.39 to -0.71 within item against law prediction -0.47 to -0.91. Models integrate candidates even after verifying them invalid (93 to 100% with propositional constraints; up to 99.4% on held-out science reasoning).
limits: Short answer-choice tasks with one or two messages, not matrices of dozens of items. Exact repeats are discounted, but near-duplicates and paraphrases were not shown to be. No matrix rating test.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: models do not simply count duplicates; they discount exact repeats and agreement adds less each time. But verified-invalid candidates still get adopted, so a verification step by the model does not control the answer. Let code, not the model, enforce rejection and dedupe.

source: Wunderlich, Kaesberg, Wahle, Ruas & Gipp (2026) Multi-agent reasoning improves compute efficiency: Pareto-optimal test-time scaling
finding: At comparable compute, debate and mixture-of-agents beat self-consistency by a small margin on MMLU-Pro. Self-refinement was always below plain chain of thought. Self-consistency saturated at about 10 samples and debate at about 4 agents.
numbers: MMLU-Pro (1,000 questions) and BBH; 34 configurations, over 100 evaluations, up to about 20x CoT compute; 70B and 8B models. CoT 64.3%; self-consistency best 68.7% (10 samples, +4.4); debate 70.0% (4 agents, 2 layers, +5.7); mixture-of-agents 71.4% (5 models, 4 layers, +7.1). Debate +1.3 and MoA +2.7 over self-consistency at comparable budget.
limits: Open Llama-class models, multiple-choice benchmarks; compute measured as generations and time. Debate here is generic exchange, not assigned dissent. Contradicts Huang 2024 and Smit 2024 on debate vs self-consistency (those found self-consistency ahead), so the sign depends on setup.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a fair equal-compute test of assigned dissent against self-consistency is still missing. The best-supported structure is parallel independent generation plus a differently-framed aggregator, not repeated rounds.

finding: Extra inference compute helps hard questions a lot and easy ones little. Hard items are those a model solves rarely over repeated plain attempts, which gives a cheap trigger.
numbers: MMLU-Pro bins by CoT solve rate over 20 attempts: easy >75% (CoT accuracy 94.4%, gain +2.2 at 15 to 20x compute), medium 25 to 75% (+8.5), hard <25% (+9.0).
limits: Bins built from 20 repeat samples per question, which costs compute itself; gain is for all pipelines pooled, not for dissent alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: sample disagreement (low solve rate across independent samples) predicts where extra structure pays. Trigger the critic or matrix only when independent samples disagree; skip it when they agree.

source: Li et al. (2026) DynaDebate: breaking homogeneity in multi-agent debate with dynamic path generation
finding: Debate agents that start from the same reasoning path copy each other's mistakes and debate collapses into majority voting. Assigning distinct solution paths before debate, and calling an external verifier only when agents disagree, gave the best results. Plain CoT-SC and generic MAD were often no better than one CoT.
numbers: Three runs, mean +/- sd. Qwen3-8B: MATH500 CoT 78.07, CoT-SC 72.87, MAD 72.20, DynaDebate 82.17; AIME24 CoT 30.00, DynaDebate 35.56; GPQA CoT 43.67, DynaDebate 46.38. Llama-3.3-70B MATH500: CoT 67.80, CoT-SC 60.27, MAD 53.20, DynaDebate 73.27. GPT-4o-mini MMLU: CoT 82.00, CoT-SC 83.00, MAD 81.33, DynaDebate 84.44. Removing diverse initialization lowers AIME24 35.56 to 28.89 and AIME25 27.78 to 21.11 but MATH500 only -1.44 and MMLU -1.22.
limits: Compute is not equalized in the table. Small and mid models, math and QA tasks. Some cells favour baselines (Self-Contrast on Llama MMLU 87.78 vs 86.96; GPT-4o-mini AIME25 16.67 vs 13.33). Gains are larger on hard problems.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 4 and 5: independent-then-diverse beats a shared-context start, most on hard items; a disagreement-triggered verifier is a working trigger design. Assign different paths to independent drafts, then merge.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: premortem reasoning for safer language models
finding: A prompt that makes the model list possible harms, analyse their consequences, and then answer under constraints (a pre-mortem style step) cut judged harmfulness more than a plain safety instruction at similar token counts. This is a safety task, not forecasting or investigation.
numbers: TRIDENT professional-ethics scenarios (harmfulness 1 to 5): zero-shot 3.22, SafetyPrompt 2.62, InvThink prompt-only 2.19 (32.0% less than zero-shot, about 16% less than SafetyPrompt); SFT variant 1.58 to 2.22.
limits: Safety, not accuracy. Harm scores come from an LLM judge. The paper also trains models, so only the prompt-only mode applies here. No forecasting or analyst task.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the only measured pre-mortem effect on a current LLM found is on safety refusals. It shows 'list the ways this fails first' beats 'be careful' at similar length, but says nothing yet about analyst-style tasks.

source: Suh, Alperin, Li & Gomez (2025) Don't just translate, agitate: LLMs as devil's advocates for AI explanations
finding: A position paper arguing LLMs should act as devil's advocates against AI explanations. It reports no experiment and no numbers.
limits: Opinion piece at a CHI 2025 workshop; no data.
agent_relevance: Do not count as evidence. Confirms gap 8: no measured test of devil's advocate or red team prompts on analyst-style LLM tasks was found.

source: Zheng, Zhou, Meng, Zhou & Huang (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors (ICLR)
finding: LLMs prefer certain option labels, so moving the correct answer to another slot changes accuracy. This is the nearest evidence on whether order and layout of candidates matter for LLMs. No study of hypothesis rows versus columns was found.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. Moving the gold answer to position D lowered gpt-3.5-turbo accuracy by 6.3 points (67.2 to 60.9). Bias is mainly tied to option ID tokens (A/B/C/D): removing option IDs cut recall spread.
limits: Older models (gpt-3.5 era) and option letters, not layout of a matrix. Human anchoring in Dhami 2024 was about rows versus columns in a table; this is a different mechanism.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open as a direct test. Practical rule: permute hypothesis order across independent samples and use code to merge, which cancels order bias.

source: Nogueira et al. (2026) Measuring opinion bias and sycophancy via LLM-based persuasion
finding: Sycophancy shows up much more under sustained argument than under direct questioning. Models that look opinionated when asked directly mirror the user under debate.
numbers: 13 assistants, 38 topics in Brazilian Portuguese. Argumentative debate triggers sycophancy 2 to 3 times as often as direct questioning (median 50% to 79%).
limits: Opinion topics (values, policy), not factual accuracy; Portuguese; LLM judge. Not about analyst tasks.
agent_relevance: A critic that argues with the draft in the same thread risks making the drafter concede. Keep the critic's output as a list of checks for code to apply, not as a debate turn.
